spoken: In eighteen seventy-four, the English economist William Stanley Jevons printed a puzzle in a book.
He asked which two numbers, multiplied together, make 8,616,460,799.
I think it unlikely, he added, that anyone but myself will ever know.
Confident.
Well, multiplying two numbers is easy. Finding them again from the answer can be very hard.
And lopsided problems like his now guard every secure web page you open.
They're what let two strangers agree on a secret while everyone listens.
This is the story of public-key cryptography, and it was invented twice.
For most of history, sending a secret message meant sharing a secret key first.
And the same key locks the message and unlocks it, so whoever has it can read everything.
So the key is the weak point.
Exactly. It had to travel safely, by trusted courier or at a face-to-face meeting.
And every pair of people who want to talk privately needs a key of their own.
Ten people need forty-five keys.
A thousand people need 499,500.
That's half a million keys to deliver.
Two researchers at Stanford called this the key distribution problem in 1976.
And their answer sounds impossible. It lets strangers agree on a key in full view of everyone.
In 1974, Whitfield Diffie, an independent researcher, was advised to meet a young Stanford professor, Martin Hellman.
They'd planned a half-hour meeting. It lasted many hours.
In November 1976, they published New Directions in Cryptography.
It opens with the line, We stand today on the brink of a revolution in cryptography.
That's quite a first line.
It held up, and they won the twenty fifteen Turing Award for it.
So what was the revolution? It was splitting the key in two.
One key locks, a different key unlocks, and knowing the first doesn't give you the second.
So you could publish your locking key like a phone number, and anyone could send you messages only you can read.
Anyone can close the lock. Only you can open it.
But for that they needed a trapdoor one-way function, which is easy to compute but hard to undo, unless you hold a secret.
And they didn't have one. The problem, they wrote, was still largely open.
So the revolution came with a hole in the middle.
A hole, yes. But they did have a way to agree on a key in public, building on ideas from Ralph Merkle.
And Hellman later said the method should carry Merkle's name too.
Let's try it in paint first. Alice and Bob agree, in public, on yellow as their starting colour.
Each mixes in a secret colour of their own, red for Alice and blue for Bob.
They swap the mixtures in the open, where Eve, listening in, sees them too.
Then each stirs in their own secret again, and they both end up with the same brown.
And Eve has the yellow and both mixtures, but she can't pull the secret colours back out.
Is the paint picture fair, though? It seems a little too perfect.
It's fair up to this point. Paint can never be unmixed, but the maths can, by trying every secret.
So the defence is sheer numbers, with far too many secrets to try.
Right. The real version uses clock arithmetic. Picture a clock with 23 hours.
Start at one and keep multiplying by five, keeping only the remainder after dividing by twenty-three.
The hand jumps to 5, then 2, then 10, then 4, then 20, with no pattern you can easily see.
It looks almost random.
Stepping forward is easy. Working back to how many steps it took is the discrete logarithm problem, and it's hard.
Now comes the exchange. Everyone, Eve included, knows twenty-three and five.
Alice secretly picks 3. After 3 steps, the hand is on 10, and she sends 10.
Bob secretly picks seven. After seven steps, the hand is on seventeen, and he sends seventeen.
Alice raises Bob's 17 to the power of her secret 3, and Bob raises Alice's 10 to the power of his 7.
And both get fourteen, because both have really taken three times seven steps from the start, which is twenty-one.
It's the same steps in a different order, just like the paint.
Meanwhile Eve heard the numbers twenty-three and five, then ten and seventeen. To reach fourteen, she needs three or seven.
With 23 hours she could try them all, so real exchanges use a prime of at least 2,048 bits, which is 617 digits.
Key exchange was a breakthrough. But a true public lock, one that anyone could close, was still missing.
At M I T, Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman spent about a year hunting for one.
Rivest and Shamir proposed ideas, and Adleman, the mathematician, kept breaking them.
Somebody has to.
Then, in April nineteen seventy-seven, after a Passover evening at a student's house, Rivest couldn't sleep.
By daybreak, the story goes, he had much of the paper written.
It's named R S A after their initials, and it starts with two prime numbers.
Let's build a tiny one. Take the primes 61 and 53, and multiply them to get 3,233.
Pick seventeen as the power that locks. From the primes, we can work out that the power that unlocks is four hundred and thirteen.
And the public key is just 3,233 and 17. Anyone can have it.
Right. To send Bob 65, raise it to the power of 17 and keep the remainder after dividing by 3,233.
That power has thirty-one digits, but only the remainder, two thousand seven hundred and ninety, travels.
Bob raises that to the power of 413, divides by 3,233 again, and out comes 65.
Wait, straight back to sixty-five?
Exactly. The two powers undo each other, if you know both.
And finding four hundred and thirteen needs the two primes. The public key shows only their product.
Real systems also add random padding. Bare R S A like this is just a demonstration.
So it all rests on a lopsided pair of jobs. Multiplying is easy, and factoring is hard.
How hard, though? A number like 3,233 doesn't look so scary.
It isn't. Try dividing by each prime in turn, and the sixteenth prime, which is fifty-three, works.
Jevons's number needs thousands of tries. It's 89,681 times 96,079.
Charles Busk found that in eighteen eighty-nine.
So much for anyone but myself.
Then, in August nineteen seventy-seven, Martin Gardner described R S A in Scientific American, along with a challenge message locked with a hundred and twenty-nine digit number.
And there was a 100 dollar prize for unlocking it.
Rivest estimated that, with the best methods of the day, a hundred and twenty-five digit number would take forty quadrillion years.
Forty quadrillion. That sounds safe.
It wasn't. Better methods came, and about six hundred volunteers, with some sixteen hundred computers, cracked it in nineteen ninety-four.
The message read, the magic words are squeamish ossifrage.
An ossifrage is a vulture, by the way. The name means bone-breaker.
So keys grew. Public factoring records are under 300 digits. A 2,048 bit key has 617.
And no one has proved that factoring is hard. There's just no fast way known on ordinary computers.
Now run the same maths the other way, and you get something just as useful, which is a signature.
Diffie and Hellman proposed digital signatures in nineteen seventy-six, and R S A made them work.
Bob locks a message with his private 413. Anyone can open it with his public 17.
But if anyone can open it, what's the point?
The point is who could have locked it. Signing 1977 gives 788, and raising 788 to the power of 17 gives back 1977.
Only the holder of four hundred and thirteen could have made seven hundred and eighty-eight, so it proves who signed.
In practice you sign a short fingerprint of the message, called a hash.
And signatures close a gap we skipped over in key exchange, one that lets an attacker sit in the middle.
Mallory sits between Alice and Bob and runs one exchange with each, posing as the other.
Each thinks they share a key with the other. Both actually share one with Mallory, who reads everything.
And neither of them would notice.
No. Plain Diffie–Hellman can't tell who is really on the other end.
On the web, the proof is a certificate, which is the site's public key, signed by an authority your browser trusts.
Now comes the twist, kept secret for more than twenty years.
In January 1970, at Britain's G C H Q, James Ellis wrote a secret report on non-secret encryption.
The idea came from a wartime Bell Labs paper, in which the receiver adds noise to a call, then removes it.
So the receiver helps lock the message.
Right. Ellis argued that it was possible, but he couldn't see a way to build it.
Then, in September 1973, a young mathematician, Clifford Cocks, joined and heard about the idea.
Cocks knew number theory. He chose prime factoring, and quickly found what we now call R S A.
He didn't even write it down at the time.
That's four years before M I T.
And in 1974, his colleague Malcolm Williamson found what we now call Diffie–Hellman key exchange.
With a military focus and little computing power, G C H Q found no use for it, and it stayed secret.
It was made public in nineteen ninety-seven, when Cocks gave a talk on the eighteenth of December.
James Ellis had died on the 25th of November, a month too soon.
And as far as anyone knows, the Stanford and M I T teams found it all on their own.
So what actually happens when you open a secure web page today?
Your browser and the server run a fresh key exchange, often on elliptic curves rather than a clock.
The server signs the exchange, and its certificate shows that the signature really is the site's.
That's the answer to Mallory.
Public-key maths is slow, so it only sets up a key; a fast ordinary cipher carries the page.
And the exchange keys are thrown away afterwards, so a key stolen later can't unlock today's traffic.
R S A keys usually have 2,048 bits or more. On elliptic curves, 256 bits does as well as 3,072.
In 1994, Peter Shor showed how a quantum computer could factor huge numbers quickly.
And his method solves discrete logarithms too, so it would break R S A and Diffie–Hellman alike.
Both of them? Should we be worried?
Not yet. No such machine exists, and demonstrations have factored only fifteen and twenty-one, helped by knowing the answer.
Breaking real keys might take millions of qubits, because of error correction.
The worry is that a message recorded today could be decrypted later. This is called harvest now, decrypt later.
So in August 2024, N I S T, the U S standards institute, published three post-quantum standards, one for keys and two for signatures.
The key one, M L Kem, rests on lattice problems, which are thought to resist quantum attacks.
And Chrome and Firefox already mix it into their key exchange, alongside a classic elliptic curve.
So strangers can agree on a key in public, because some sums are easy one way and hard the other.
A lock can be public, if only its owner knows the trapdoor.
And run backwards, the same maths signs.
Jevons was wrong about his number, but right that some sums are far easier done than undone.
And every secure connection begins that way, with two strangers, in public, agreeing on a secret only they know.
